exercises.prompt: Implement square_map(n) so it returns a dict mapping each integer i from 1 to n (inclusive) to its square i*i — square_map(3) is {1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9}. When n is 0 (or less) there are no integers to map, so it returns an empty dict.
exercises.solution:
def square_map(n):
    return {i: i * i for i in range(1, n + 1)}
hints: A dict comprehension has the shape {key: value for ...}, building both sides of each entry as it iterates.
range(1, n + 1) counts i from 1 through n inclusive; map each i to i * i.
return {i: i * i for i in range(1, n + 1)} — for n of 0, range(1, 1) is empty, so you get {} with no special case.

exercises.prompt: Implement invert_dict(d) so it returns a new dict with keys and values swapped, built as a single dict comprehension: each value becomes a key mapping back to its original key. invert_dict({'a': 1, 'b': 2}) is {1: 'a', 2: 'b'}. Assume the values are unique and usable as keys. An empty dict returns an empty dict.
exercises.solution:
def invert_dict(d):
    return {value: key for key, value in d.items()}
hints: You inverted a dict with a loop before; a dict comprehension does the same swap in one line.
Iterate the pairs with d.items() and put value first, key second: {value: key for key, value in d.items()}.
return {value: key for key, value in d.items()} — the original values become the new keys.

exercises.prompt: Implement keep_high(d, threshold) so it returns a new dict holding only the entries of d whose value is greater than or equal to threshold, keys unchanged. keep_high({'a': 1, 'b': 5, 'c': 3}, 3) is {'b': 5, 'c': 3}. An empty dict, or one where no value reaches threshold, returns an empty dict.
exercises.solution:
def keep_high(d, threshold):
    return {key: value for key, value in d.items() if value >= threshold}
hints: A dict comprehension can filter as well as build — add a trailing if to decide which entries survive.
Keep the whole entry when its value clears the bar: {key: value for key, value in d.items() if value >= threshold}.
return {key: value for key, value in d.items() if value >= threshold} — >= keeps a value exactly equal to threshold.

exercises.prompt: Implement from_pairs(keys, values) so it pairs the two lists element-wise into a dict — the first key maps to the first value, and so on. from_pairs(['a', 'b', 'c'], [1, 2, 3]) is {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}. If the lists differ in length, stop at the shorter one. Two empty lists return an empty dict.
exercises.solution:
def from_pairs(keys, values):
    return {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}
hints: zip walks the two lists in lockstep, handing you one key and one value at a time, and stops at the shorter list.
Feed those pairs into a dict comprehension: {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}.
return {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)} — or equivalently dict(zip(keys, values)); zip stopping early handles the mismatched-length cases.

exercises.prompt: Implement scale_values(d, factor) so it returns a new dict with the same keys as d but every value multiplied by factor. scale_values({'a': 1, 'b': 2}, 10) is {'a': 10, 'b': 20}. The keys are unchanged. An empty dict returns an empty dict.
exercises.solution:
def scale_values(d, factor):
    return {key: value * factor for key, value in d.items()}
hints: You keep every key but transform its value, so this is a dict comprehension that rebuilds each entry.
Iterate the pairs and multiply the value: {key: value * factor for key, value in d.items()}.
return {key: value * factor for key, value in d.items()} — the keys pass through untouched while each value scales.
